title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 20: Social Weather Stations v. Comelec: May Election Surveys Be Banned?
keywords: freedom of expression is a preferred right
equal access to opportunities for public service
primary_topics: Chapter 20 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's report on Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, in which the Court struck down Section 5.4 of RA 9006 (the Fair Elections Act) banning the publication of election surveys fifteen days before a national and seven days before a local election, as 'an unconstitutional abridgment of freedom of speech, expression and the press'

A continuation of the free-expression line he began as ponente in ABS-CBN v. Comelec (the exit-poll case): the survey ruling, he wrote, strengthened his 'elation and confidence in the Court's capacity to resolve questions impinging on new modes of free speech'

A doctrinal walk-through of the Mendoza ponencia's application of the United States v. O'Brien test -- Section 5.4 failing criterion [3] because it suppressed a whole class of expression while leaving columnists and commentators free, and criterion [4] because its aims could be pursued more narrowly by punishing unlawful acts rather than speech

A survey of the separate opinions: the concurrences of Justices Melo (prior restraint, citing Fr. Bernas) and Puno (clear and present danger and overbreadth), CJP's own concurrence grounding the result on freedom of expression as a preferred right, and Justice Kapunan's dissent balancing free speech against 'equal access to opportunities for public service' and the bandwagon effect
sub_topics: The starting point: in ABS-CBN v. Comelec, which CJP had 'the honor of writing for the Court,' the Comelec was held unable to totally prohibit exit polls and the dissemination of their results, exit polls being part of constitutionally protected free expression, decided 10-4 with one abstention

The parties and the challenged provision: SWS, a private nonstock nonprofit social research institution, with Kamahalan Publishing Corporation (publisher of Manila Standard), sought to stop the Comelec from enforcing Section 5.4 of RA 9006, which barred publication of surveys on national candidates 15 days and on local candidates 7 days before an election

The holding: in a 7-5-3 ponencia by Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, the Court held Section 5.4 an unconstitutional abridgment because it laid a prior restraint, and because the Comelec's power under Art. IX-C, Section 4 is limited to ensuring 'equal opportunity, time, space, and the right to reply' and to prescribing uniform and reasonable rates

The O'Brien test as 'the most influential test for distinguishing content-based from content-neutral regulations,' with its four criteria, and the rule that a law falls if the governmental interest is 'not unrelated to the suppression of free expression' or if the restriction exceeds what is necessary

First failure (criterion 3): the ban 'suppresses a whole class of expression' while allowing columnists, radio and TV commentators and 'armchair theorists' to opine on the same subject, showing a bias for personal opinion over statistical results; the limited period does not save it because the curtailment is 'direct, absolute, and substantial'

The distinction from National Press Club and Osmena: the RA 6646 Section 11(b) ban was authorized by a specific constitutional provision and supplied an alternative -- Comelec space and Comelec hour -- so there was no ban but only a substitution

Second failure (criterion 4): the aims of preventing last-minute pressure, the bandwagon effect, junking of losing candidates and 'dagdag-bawas' are praiseworthy but can be pursued more narrowly by punishing unlawful acts rather than speech

The concurrences: Justice Melo, who had dissented in ABS-CBN, called Section 5.4 plain prior restraint carrying 'a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity' (citing Fr. Joaquin Bernas), and warned that the possibility of abuse by some survey firms cannot justify restricting all of them; Justice Puno invoked Schenk v. United States, the clear and present danger rule and the overbreadth doctrine, noting the ban does not distinguish reliable surveys from sloppy or misleading ones

CJP's own Concurring Opinion, resting heavily on his ABS-CBN ponencia: freedom of expression is a preferred right standing on a higher level than other substantive liberties; limits require a clear and present danger of substantive character; neither Congress nor the Comelec showed one; and Daily Herald Co. v. Munro held the state's general interest in insulating voters from outside influences insufficient

Justice Kapunan's dissent: two conflicting interests -- free speech and 'equal access to opportunities for public service' -- required the Court to weigh and balance; Congress did not exceed constitutional limits; surveys work as 'a self-fulfilling prophecy' and are uniquely persuasive because they are 'clothed with the mantle of statistics'; many countries impose similar bans of varying lengths; and the Court should not substitute its judgment for that of Congress

CJP's closing explanation of the voting: Justices Melo, Vitug and Mendoza had dissented in ABS-CBN only because that Decision came after the elections and was 'technically moot,' yet all voted in favor of SWS -- with the ABS-CBN ponencia itself having brushed aside mootness because the issue's 'implications on the people's fundamental freedom of expression transcend the past election'
signature_phrases: the Court could meet headon new paradigms of free expression brought about by the advances of science and technology
My elation and confidence in the Court's capacity to resolve questions impinging on new modes of free speech
the freedom of expression is a preferred right, standing on a higher level than other substantive liberties
the evil sought to be avoided must be so substantive as to justify a clamp over one's mouth or a restraint of a writing instrument
No lover of freedom, no guardian of the Constitution and no advocate of democracy can agree to this unreasonable restraint.

stances.claim: A statutory ban on publishing election surveys in the days before an election is an unconstitutional prior restraint: the curtailment of expression is 'direct, absolute, and substantial' and is not made less so because it lasts only fifteen or seven days.
stances.rhetorical_move: reports and endorses the ponencia's application of the O'Brien test, showing the ban fails criteria [3] and [4]

stances.claim: Freedom of expression is a preferred right standing on a higher level than other substantive liberties, so any limitation must be justified by a clear and present danger of substantive character -- a danger neither Congress nor the Comelec was able to show for election surveys.
stances.rhetorical_move: quotes his own Concurring Opinion, which relied on his earlier ABS-CBN ponencia, and closes with the rhetorical appeal that no lover of freedom could accept the restraint

stances.claim: The Court is able to meet the new paradigms of free expression created by advances in science and technology -- exit polls in ABS-CBN, statistical surveys in SWS -- rather than treating novel media as outside constitutional protection.
stances.rhetorical_move: reads two of his own free-expression cases as a single developing line, using his 'elation' at the first to frame the second

stances.claim: Justice Kapunan's contrary position -- that the conflict between free speech and 'equal access to opportunities for public service' should be resolved in favor of Congress, because surveys operate as a self-fulfilling prophecy and many countries impose similar bans -- was the dissent's case.
stances.rhetorical_move: reproduces the dissent at length and without rebuttal, leaving it as the recorded opposing view

notable_anecdotes: He recalls his 'elation' at the 10-4 vote (with one abstention) in ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit-poll decision he 'had the honor of writing for the Court' and had already reported in his earlier book Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity?
He notes with evident satisfaction that Justice Melo, who had dissented in ABS-CBN, concurred here that Section 5.4 'plainly constitutes prior restraint on the freedom of expression.'
He recounts Justice Puno singling out SWS as 'one of our more reliable private nonstock, nonprofit social research institutions with a no-nonsense record,' yet barred by an overbroad provision.

He closes by explaining the apparent switch of Justices Melo, Vitug and Mendoza -- their ABS-CBN dissents rested on mootness because that decision came after the elections -- and quotes the ABS-CBN ponencia's own answer that the issue 'transcend[s] the past election.'
target_audience: Students and practitioners of constitutional law tracing the free-expression and prior-restraint doctrines in Philippine election cases
Journalists, pollsters and media organizations whose work is touched by election-period regulation
Readers of the centenary volume following the Court's handling of new modes of speech

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reported the Supreme Court's decision in Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, which struck down Section 5.4 of RA 9006, the Fair Elections Act, barring publication of election surveys fifteen days before a national and seven days before a local election. CJP opened by recalling ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit-poll case he had written for the Court and reported in an earlier book, where he had expressed elation at the 10-4 vote because it showed the Court could meet head-on new paradigms of free expression brought about by advances in science and technology; the survey case, he wrote, strengthened that confidence. He set out the challenged provision and the statutory definition of an election survey, then reproduced the 7-5-3 ponencia of Justice Vicente V. Mendoza holding the ban an unconstitutional abridgment of speech, expression and the press: it laid a prior restraint, the Comelec's constitutional powers over media reach only equal opportunity, time, space and the right to reply, and under the United States v. O'Brien test the provision failed criterion three, since it suppressed a whole class of expression while leaving columnists and commentators free to opine, and criterion four, since aims such as preventing last-minute pressure, the bandwagon effect and dagdag-bawas could be pursued by punishing unlawful acts rather than speech. He distinguished National Press Club and Osmena, where the ad ban had constitutional authorization and supplied Comelec space and Comelec hour as a substitute. He then summarized the concurrences of Justice Melo, who had dissented in ABS-CBN, and of Justice Puno, who invoked the clear and present danger rule and the overbreadth doctrine, and quoted his own concurrence treating freedom of expression as a preferred right limitable only upon a substantive danger. He reproduced Justice Kapunan's dissent on balancing free speech against equal access to public service, and closed by explaining that the earlier ABS-CBN dissents had rested only on mootness.
